s.en: When she woke, her whole body was heavy as lead.
It had long been light outside, and from downstairs came the sound of gears being polished.
She'd overslept. But Oz hadn't come up to bellow at her.
Combing her hair in front of the mirror, Sera suddenly stopped.
Among her chestnut hair, a single strand of white.
From root to tip, white as if touched by frost.
"For every bit of time you turn back, your own time gets whittled away."
Her mother's words from the echo rang once more in the back of her mind.
She pinched it between her fingers to pull it out, then stopped.
Pulling it out wasn't going to bring the lost time back.
And besides, it was proof of a choice she had made herself.
There might be reasons to hide it, but she didn't feel there was any reason to throw it away.
When she came downstairs, Oz looked up from the workbench.
For the briefest moment, her grandfather's gaze rested on her hair.
"...Food's in the kitchen. Eat it before it goes cold."
That was all he said before going back to work.
Sera understood that not asking was her grandfather's own way of being kind.
That day's workshop was taking apart and reassembling a steam valve.
Normally she could do it with her eyes shut, but today her fingers wouldn't do what she wanted.
Three times she failed to tighten a screw. Twice she fitted a part in upside down.
"Miss Milford."
The moment the closing bell rang, Instructor Regen called out to her.
"Once you've tidied up, please come to my office."
Niko threw her a worried look. Sera gave a small shake of her head to signal she was fine.
The Mechanics instructor's office was at the very back of the workshop building.
The instant she opened the door, the sound of countless seconds ticking enveloped her like rain.
Every wall, every shelf, was crowded with clocks.
Mantel clocks and wall clocks, marine chronometers, pocket watches taken apart with their insides laid bare.
Every last one of them showed exactly the same time.
"Have a seat. I can't even offer you tea, I'm afraid."
Instructor Regen pushed a mountain of papers on his desk to one side.
"Now. I'll ask you plainly. What did you do inside the tower that day?"
A cold sweat ran down Sera's back.
"...Nothing. I was just lucky."
"Luck, was it."
Luck alone could not have started you running before the gear fell — those sleepy eyes said as much.
He took a sheet of paper from his desk drawer.
It was a chart crammed with tiny figures and undulating lines.
"These are readings from recording devices I've fitted to clock towers all across Vern."
"At the moment of the accident, in the area around the tower and nowhere else, time ran backwards for roughly nine seconds."
"And the person at the centre of it..."
He tapped one point on the chart with a fingertip.
There was no wriggling out of it.
Sera bit her lip and looked down.
"There's no need to worry. I have no intention of reporting this to anyone."
Surprised, she looked up — and he was faintly smiling.
"Elise and I were classmates, you see. We studied side by side."
"You... and my mother?"
"She was a brilliant engineer. I couldn't hold a candle to her."
He turned the chart over. Another graph was drawn on the back.
A straight line, sloping steadily downward.
"This is the record for the last ten years. Every day, Vern loses about three seconds."
"Three seconds...?"
"Three seconds a day, nobody notices. It's just a margin of error."
"But pile it up over ten years and it's more than three hours."
"Where is that time disappearing to? That's what Elise was investigating."
"And one night, she was gone."
Every clock in the room struck noon at once.
He waited for the chimes to stop, then said quietly:
"Miss Milford. Be careful of House Eisen."
"Viola... she's on our side."
"Whether she herself is, I can't say. But the only ones in this city who can lay a hand on the time crystal are House Eisen."
"Whoever's hands the lost time is passing into, it's almost impossible that that family knows nothing about it."
"The enemy of your enemy isn't necessarily your friend."
As she went to leave, he added one more thing.
"And — that white hair, too. Think carefully about what you're giving up each time you turn back time."
Sera's hand went to her hair before she could stop it.
Dinner at the House of Eisen was always quiet.
Father and daughter sat facing each other from opposite ends of a long table.
Since her mother's death, that had become the ordinary state of things.
As the servers changed the plates without a sound, all that could be heard was the touch of silver on china.
"Viola."
Once the soup plates had been cleared, her father — Walter Eisen — spoke.
"Where did you go last night?"
Viola's hand paused, ever so slightly.

t: 休ませていただきました
s.en: "I went nowhere at all. I retired early."
"I see."
Her father asked nothing further.
Not because he believed her. He simply wasn't interested.
For as long as she could remember, her father's attention had been turned to nothing but the Great Clock and the honour of House Eisen.
"More importantly, you will attend next week's council meeting with me."
"The council? Me?"

t: 覚えていただかねばならん
s.en: "You will inherit the Great Clock one day. The gentlemen of the House of Lords must learn your face."
"...As you wish."
That evening's guest was the Countess Rosenberg.
The countess, who must be past eighty, looked forty at most.
Firm skin, glossy black hair, a laugh as clear as a girl's.
Not only was she youthful — each time they met, she seemed to have grown a little younger still.
Society called it "the miracle beauty," but ever since she was small, Viola had felt an indescribable chill whenever she came near the countess.
Her chronomancer's skin told her something was wrong.
Around the countess, and only there, the flow of time was somehow stagnant.
"Walter, darling — you'll be sending the usual this month as well, I trust?"
"But of course, Countess. On the name of House Eisen."
Her father smiled gently.
It was a smile even his own daughter had barely ever seen.
What was "the usual"?
Once dinner was over and the mansion had fallen asleep, Viola slipped out of her room.
A dressing gown over her nightclothes and not so much as a candle, she made her way down the dark corridor.
Her goal: her father's study.
In front of the door, the old butler on night duty sat in a chair, nodding off.
Viola opened her fan and gently stretched out the time around the old man.
One second into ten, ten into a hundred.
The old butler's half-closed eyelids stayed just as they were, barely moving at all.
"...Forgive me, Hans."
With that whispered apology, Viola slipped into the study.
This was the second time she had crept into her father's study.
The first had been when she was twelve. The night she found that scorched old document.
The desk drawer was locked, but the key's hiding place hadn't changed since then.
Under the base of the globe.
Her father wasn't just meticulous — he was astonishingly set in his habits.
Inside the drawer was a single leather-bound ledger.
On the cover, stamped in gold leaf: "Time Shards — Delivery Records."
With trembling fingers, Viola turned the pages.
Date, family name, quantity, and price.
House Rosenberg. House Weiss. House Graf.
The names of Vern's most illustrious nobility filled page after page.
Time shards — small slivers carved from the time crystal.
Wear one, it was said, and ageing would slow.
And yet that was supposed to be the very thing House Eisen, guardian of the crystal, had forbidden most strictly of all.
Carve the crystal, and you carve away the city's time.
Any child knew that much.
"...This cannot be."
The date on the last page was three days ago.
Out in the corridor, a floorboard creaked.
Viola's head jerked up.
The spell on the butler was coming undone.
There was no time to hesitate.
Viola tore out just the last page, put the ledger back exactly as it had been, and leapt from the window into the moonlit garden.
Niko's home was an old flat-bottomed barge afloat on the canal.
Father, mother, and five younger siblings: eight people crammed together in a cramped cabin.
"Niko, you're late!"
The instant he hopped aboard, Toma, his next-youngest brother, started grumbling.
"We were about to eat all the dinner without you."
"Sorry, sorry. Had a bit of business."
Niko ruffled his brother's hair and squeezed himself in at the narrow table.
In the pot, the usual bean and potato stew.
Their mother ladled it out into each plate with a big ladle.
"Niko, what are you up to at that Academy lately? Sneaking out in the middle of the night."
"I'm not up to anything. Studying. Studying."
"Liar. I've never once seen you studying."
His brothers and sisters burst out laughing, and Niko laughed it off too.
Mina, the youngest, sat on their mother's lap, holding a tin music box as if it were treasure.
Niko had made it for her out of scavenged scrap; wind it up and it played a slightly off-key lullaby.
"Big bruvver, wind it."
"Right you are, leave it to me."
Niko wound it, Mina's eyes crinkled with delight — and that was when it happened.
The barge stopped.
No — not just the barge.
The flickering lamp flame, the steam, the broth about to drip from his mother's ladle: all perfectly still.
The music box's tune, too, hung broken off mid-note.
A time-tremor.
For a split second he wondered if he alone could move. He couldn't.
Not one finger, not one eyelid would move.
Only his mind remained, locked inside a frozen body.
One second. Two. Three.
They felt as long as forever.
Then, abruptly, the world moved again.
The broth fell into the plate, the lamp flame wavered, the music box played on.
Not one of his family had noticed anything happen.
Only Mina was staring at her music box, baffled.
"...Bruvver. The song stopped just now."
Niko couldn't answer.
He took his little sister's small hand. It was warm.
That seemed, suddenly, an enormous blessing.
— How many more times will this happen?
— And what if, one day, it never starts again?
"...Can't leave this be."
Niko murmured it too quietly for anyone to hear.
The next morning, the three met at Niko's warehouse.
Viola laid a sheet of paper on the wooden crate that served as their table.
The page torn from the ledger.
Dates and family names, quantities and prices, entered in meticulous handwriting.
"Time shards..."
Niko grimaced.
"I've heard of 'em. The stones the nobs up top supposedly pay a fortune for to live longer, right?"
"I had thought it nothing more than a rumour. Until last night."
Viola's voice was calm.
Too calm. It was painful to hear.
Sera told them what she'd heard from Instructor Regen.
Time lost at three seconds a day. Three hours over ten years. And her mother, who'd been looking into it.
When she finished, a heavy silence fell over the warehouse.
"...In other words."
Viola was the first to speak.
"The one stealing the city's time is my father — House Eisen. Is that what you're saying?"
No one could answer right away.
"It's not settled yet."
Niko spoke slowly, for once choosing his words.
"Even if they're definitely selling time shards, that alone doesn't mean they've carved off three hours in ten years. The numbers might not add up."
"Mr. Niko..."
"Numbers don't lie. If we're gonna check, we do the maths properly first."
Viola stared at Niko, wide-eyed, and then the corners of her mouth softened, just a little.
"...You say surprisingly sensible things."
"You can drop the 'surprisingly'."
Sera took out the pocket watch.
The backward second hand was counting something back down, one mark at a time, as it did every day.
Had her mother known the answer to this?
Was it precisely because she knew that she'd gone a hundred years back?
"Let's find out. The three of us."
At Sera's words, the other two nodded in silence.
